idiom_name: Future { } on an ExecutionContext + Future.sequence/Await (parallel collections for loop-shaped splits)
implementation_notes: scala.concurrent supplies both ends: Future { task } starts each subtask on the ExecutionContext (the global one is a ForkJoinPool with a parallelism level of Runtime.availableProcessors), and the master aggregates with Future.sequence plus a map over the results - non-blocking - or blocks once with Await.result; combinators keep the fan-out compositional. Blocking work inside a future must be wrapped in scala.concurrent.blocking (or run on a dedicated ExecutionContext), and parallel collections (.par) cover regular loop decomposition without an explicit fan-out; the classic master object is needed only when the worker set must outlive the call.
code_sketch:
given ExecutionContext = ExecutionContext.global
val futures: Seq[Future[Long]] = parts.map(p => Future(partialSum(p)))
val total: Long = Await.result(Future.sequence(futures).map(_.sum), 30.seconds)
pitfalls: The global ExecutionContext is a ForkJoinPool sized to the available processors: long blocking calls starve it unless wrapped in blocking {} or moved to a dedicated pool.
Future.sequence fails fast on the first failed future and discards the successful partials; collect Try per future if the aggregate must degrade.
Await.result throws the first failure as-is and hides which subtask produced it; aggregating with combinators keeps the failure in the future instead.
